No.57

Knowing We Should Not Cling, Yet Always Unable to Do It

Knowing that attachment brings suffering does not mean one can let go at once. Growth is not never erring, but admitting mistakes, noticing attachment, and having the courage to turn back.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

🔶 I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva:

"I humbly ask: A friend says that life is so hard. In thought they know they should not cling, yet when a test comes they are knocked back to where they began. On many matters they always want a definite answer, and if things go badly, that also gives them an excuse to escape. Why is growth and change so difficult?"

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

"Good man, you should know: all beings know that attachment makes people suffer, yet to know this principle is not necessarily to be able to let go at once. For understanding is in the mind, and habitual tendencies are in the mind as well; though understanding may be clear, habitual tendencies are formed over years and months. When daily circumstances run smoothly, one thinks one is already able to let go; but the moment adversity comes, craving, fear, doubt and unease arise once more.

This is not because practice has made no progress,
but because habitual tendencies not yet truly tamed
appear again when causes and conditions come together.
Good man, the person you speak of
always wants a definite answer,
because the heart is uneasy and seeks to dispel fear through certainty.
When things do not go as hoped,
they again find reasons and a way out for themselves,
perhaps from fear of bearing failure,
or perhaps from unwillingness to face their own true choice.

Yet you should understand: in life one cannot always obtain an answer to everything, and practice does not wait until the outcome is clear before it is willing to move forward. If one must be certain of everything before daring to act, one is easily trapped by fear. If one looks for an excuse whenever things go badly, it is hard to see where one truly needs to change. True growth is not never making mistakes again, but, after a mistake, being willing to admit it; when attachment arises again, being able to notice it; when the mind turns toward escape, still having the courage to turn back.

You need not demand of yourself to become a Buddha in a single day, nor deny yesterday's effort because you have slipped back today. Practice is like tilling a field: what is sown today cannot be harvested tomorrow. Tend it day after day, weed it day after day; even if wind and rain come now and then, do not give up the work. To know attachment is the beginning of awakening; to see attachment is the work of practice; and when attachment arises, to no longer be carried wholly away by it is progress."

🔶Plain Rendering

Good man, you should know: all beings know that attachment makes people suffer, but knowing this principle does not mean one can let go right away. Understanding is in the mind, and so are habitual tendencies; even when understanding has become clear, habitual tendencies have been formed over many years. When daily circumstances run smoothly, one thinks one is already able to let go; but once adversity comes, craving, fear, doubt and unease arise again.

This does not mean practice has made no progress at all, but that habitual tendencies not yet truly tamed appear again when causes and conditions come together. Good man, the person you speak of always wants a definite answer, because they feel uneasy inside and want to use "certainty" to dispel their fear. When things do not go as hoped, they again find reasons and a way out for themselves, perhaps because they fear bearing failure, or perhaps because they are unwilling to face their own true choice.

But you should understand: in life one cannot get an answer to everything, and practice does not wait until the outcome is clear before moving forward. If one must be certain about everything before daring to act, one is easily trapped by fear. If one looks for an excuse whenever things go badly, it is hard to see where one truly needs to change. True growth is not never making mistakes again, but, after a mistake, being willing to admit it; when attachment arises again, being able to notice it; when the mind wants to escape, still having the courage to turn back.

You do not need to demand of yourself to become a Buddha in a single day, nor deny yesterday's effort because you slipped back today. Practice is like tilling a field: what you sow today cannot be harvested tomorrow. Tend it every day, weed it every day, and even if wind and rain come now and then, do not give up the work. To know attachment is the beginning of awakening; to see attachment is the work of practice; and when attachment arises, no longer being carried wholly away by it is progress.
